passages.t: A boy king who did not turn aside
passages.happening:
Josiah is eight years old when he becomes king, and he reigns thirty-one years in Jerusalem. His mother is Jedidah of Bozkath (verse 1). ‘And he did what was right in the eyes of the LORD and walked in all the ways of his father David; he did not turn aside to the right or to the left’ (verse 2).

In his eighteenth year he sends Shaphan the scribe to the house of the LORD. The high priest Hilkiah is to count the money the doorkeepers have collected from the people and hand it to the supervisors, who will pay the carpenters, builders and masons and buy timber and dressed stone to repair the temple (verses 3-6). ‘But they need not account for the money put into their hands, since they work with integrity’ (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 21 ended with Jerusalem's fate sealed under Manasseh and Amon murdered. Into that darkness comes a child king who becomes the most wholehearted reformer in Judah's history. The narrator's verdict is the highest possible, and its words, not turning aside to the right or to the left, echo the law's instructions for a king.

Josiah reigned about 640 to 609 BC, so his eighteenth year was about 622 BC. Assyria was weakening. After Ashurbanipal's death around 631 BC the empire fell into internal conflict, and Babylon rose against it. That gave Judah room to act more independently, in religion too. Jeremiah began preaching in Josiah's thirteenth year, and Zephaniah also dates his preaching to this reign.

The collection at the doors follows the system Joash set up generations earlier, and the note that the workers needed no audit because they were honest repeats the words of that account.
passages.later: The law said a king was to read God's instruction ‘all the days of his life’ (Deuteronomy 17:19), so that ‘he will not turn aside from the commandment, to the right or to the left’ (Deuteronomy 17:20).
passages.asks: Josiah was eight when he became king, and he did not turn aside. Ask what it means that God can raise up faithfulness from a family like Manasseh's and Amon's. And ask what young person near you might need your trust and your example.

passages.t: A book found in the temple
passages.happening:
Hilkiah the high priest says to Shaphan, “I have found the Book of the Law in the house of the LORD!” (verse 8). He gives it to Shaphan, who reads it. Shaphan goes to the king and reports first on the money, and then, ‘Hilkiah the priest has given me a book’ (verse 10). He reads it to the king.

‘When the king heard the words of the Book of the Law, he tore his clothes’ (verse 11). He sends Hilkiah, Shaphan, Shaphan's son Ahikam and two other officials: “Go and inquire of the LORD for me, for the people, and for all Judah concerning the words in this book that has been found. For great is the wrath of the LORD that burns against us because our fathers have not obeyed the words of this book by doing all that is written about us” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The chapter moves from routine to crisis. It opens with the ordinary business of temple repair, and then Hilkiah's announcement breaks in. Shaphan's report is almost comically understated: first the money, then, as if in passing, a book.

What the book was has been discussed since ancient times. Many early Christian and Jewish interpreters, and most modern scholars, identify it with Deuteronomy or a core of it, because Josiah's reforms in the next chapter follow Deuteronomy's commands so closely. Readers who hold that Moses wrote it see it as an old copy of the law lost during Manasseh's reign. Many critical scholars think it was written or revised not long before and presented as ancient. The text says only that it was found. Temples in the ancient world were built with foundation deposits, and kings who restored them sometimes reported finding older writings during the work, so a document found during repairs would not have seemed strange.

The word for law, torah, means instruction or teaching, not only legal rules, and it came to name the five books of Moses. Its rediscovery shows how far Judah had drifted from the terms of its covenant. Shaphan and his family appear again and again in Jeremiah. His son Ahikam protected Jeremiah from execution. Clay seal impressions from Jerusalem bear names like those of this court, including one of a Gemariah son of Shaphan, whom Jeremiah also names.
passages.later: In a later crisis, ‘Ahikam son of Shaphan supported Jeremiah, so he was not handed over to the people to be put to death’ (Jeremiah 26:24). A psalm says, ‘Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path’ (Psalm 119:105).
passages.asks: The Book of the Law had been lost inside the temple itself. Ask how a community can keep its buildings and routines while losing the word of God. And ask when God's word last made you tear your clothes, or at least stop and grieve.

passages.happening:
The officials go to Huldah the prophetess, wife of Shallum, keeper of the wardrobe, who lives in the Second District of Jerusalem (verse 14). She gives them the LORD's word. The LORD will bring disaster on this place and its people, according to all the words of the book the king has read, ‘because they have forsaken Me and burned incense to other gods’ (verse 17). His wrath will not be quenched.

But for the king who sent them she has another word. ‘Because your heart was tender and you humbled yourself before the LORD when you heard what I spoke against this place and against its people’ (verse 19), and because he tore his clothes and wept, the LORD has heard him. ‘Therefore I will indeed gather you to your fathers, and you will be gathered to your grave in peace. Your eyes will not see all the calamity that I will bring on this place’ (verse 20). They take her answer back to the king.
passages.hearers:
To inquire of the LORD meant to seek a prophet's word. Josiah's officials, the high priest among them, go not to Jeremiah or Zephaniah but to Huldah, a woman prophet whose authority they plainly respect, and her word is received as the LORD's own. The Old Testament names other women prophets, among them Miriam and Deborah. The Second District was probably a newer part of Jerusalem on the western hill that grew in the late eighth and seventh centuries, perhaps with refugees from the north after Samaria fell. Her husband kept the wardrobe, probably the temple's or the palace's vestments.

Her oracle has two parts, each introduced by the words this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: judgment on the place and people, and mercy for the king. The word heard ties the chapter together. The king heard the words of the book, and the LORD says he has heard the king. The word for tender, rakhakh, means soft, responsive, the opposite of the stiff neck that ruined Israel. What God valued in Josiah was first not his achievements but a heart that could still be moved by his word.

The chapter is honest from the start. The reform will not cancel the judgment already announced. It will show what repentance looks like, and give Judah one more generation of faithfulness.
passages.later: The book of Judges says, ‘Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time’ (Judges 4:4). Jeremiah, who began preaching in Josiah's reign, promised a new covenant: ‘I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts’ (Jeremiah 31:33).
passages.hard:
Huldah promised that Josiah would go to his grave in peace, but he was killed in battle. Was her prophecy wrong?

In the next chapter Josiah is killed at Megiddo by Pharaoh Neco, which seems hard to square with being gathered to his grave in peace. Several answers are offered. The most common is that verse 20 says what it means: Josiah's eyes would not see the disaster coming on Jerusalem. He died before the Babylonian invasions and the city's destruction, and he was buried in Jerusalem while it still stood, which is peace in the sense promised. Some add that being gathered to one's fathers in peace refers to honorable burial rather than to the manner of death.

Other readers think the tension is real and was left in place on purpose, since Kings was put together after both events and could easily have smoothed it over. They suggest the promise depended on Josiah's continued humility, and Chronicles says he died after refusing to heed a warning from God that came through Neco. On any reading the narrator did not hide the difficulty, and the promise that Josiah would not see Jerusalem fall came true.
passages.asks: Josiah's heart was tender when he heard God's word. Ask what hardens a heart against Scripture, and what keeps it soft. And ask why faithfulness is worth pursuing even when it cannot change the larger outcome.
